query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, a controlled addition of a reactive element X (Si, Mn, or Al) promotes selective surface oxidation that forms a continuous, coherent sub-scale oxide layer rich in the X-derived oxide. This layer effectively limits further oxidation by reducing oxygen diffusivity and internal stress buildup, thereby preventing cracking or spallation at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single or multiphase solid-solution state with a defined amount of X (Si, Mn, or Al) and minimal pre-existing oxides.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy specimens to high-temperature oxidative or corrosive environments (≥900 °C) under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (above 900 °C) exposure in a controlled oxidative atmosphere (and/or corrosive media) with consistent oxygen availability.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, coherent, sub-scale oxide layer enriched in the X-derived oxide (e.g., Al2O3 if X is Al or analogous oxides if X is Si or Mn) that bonds well with the underlying metal matrix.
generation.mechanism: The reactive element X preferentially oxidizes to form a slow-growing and adherent oxide layer. This layer acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, reducing further oxidation and minimizing thermal stresses that would otherwise lead to cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an effective concentration of the reactive element X will develop a stable, slow-growing, and adherent protective oxide layer, demonstrating minimal cracking or spallation compared to baseline alloys lacking X. This enhanced stability should be observable in reduced oxide layer growth rates and lower incidences of mechanical failure at the oxide–metal interface.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloy without the addition of the targeted reactive element X.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidative or corrosive conditions and is contingent on the uniform distribution and proper phase state of the reactive element X. Effects may differ with variations in X type (Si, Mn, or Al) and concentration.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the critical concentration threshold of X needed to form a fully continuous and protective oxide layer, as well as variations in the effectiveness of different X elements (Si vs Mn vs Al) under identical conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNi alloys with controlled and varied additions of X (Si, Mn, or Al) alongside a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy without X. Subject all samples to identical high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions (≥900 °C) for a fixed duration. Characterize the surface oxide layers using techniques such as SEM, TEM, XRD, and oxidation kinetics measurements.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate
Phase composition of the oxide layer (e.g., presence of X-derived oxides)
Coherence and adhesion of the oxide layer (e.g., via scratch or bend tests)
Extent of cracking or spallation observed on the surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with added X do not consistently demonstrate a more continuous, slow-growing, and adherent oxide layer relative to the baseline alloy without X—or if the protective oxide layer still shows significant cracking/spallation under identical conditions—the hypothesis will be falsified.
